Huge Buffer Pool - L2PSP
THIS IS A SECURITY CONTROL, NOT A PERFORMANCE TIER. Do not delete it because it looks unused.
ReadHandler.handleHeader:92 reads the inbound packet length as
Short.toUnsignedInt(buffer.getShort()) - ConnectionConfig.HEADER_SIZE
and checks it only for > 0 at :93, so an attacker fully controls a dataSize in 1..65533 with
NO account, NO valid client, before decryption and before opcode dispatch, on BOTH the game
and login ports. That value reaches ResourcePool.determineBufferSize:153, and when
_bufferPools.ceilingEntry(size) returns null (:155) the engine MINTS A NEW PERMANENT POOL at
:168 which is never evicted. With the stock top tier at 32768, every size in 32769..65533 is
a distinct pool: 32,765 of them, each banking a direct buffer on disconnect
(Connection.close -> releaseReadingBuffer -> recycleBuffer -> BufferPool.recycle). Sum n for
n = 32769..65533 = 1,610,432,515 bytes = 1.50 GiB of off-heap memory, permanently, for about
65 KB of traffic: connect, send 2 bytes, hang up, repeat.
A pool whose BufferSize covers the WHOLE representable range means ceilingEntry never returns
null on the read path, so neither ResourcePool.determineBufferSize:168 nor
ResourcePool.getSizedBuffer:139 ever puts into the map from an inbound packet again. 32,765
permanent pools become one, ~1.5 GiB of permanent leak becomes 4 x 64 KB = 256 KB, and the
unsynchronised TreeMap at ResourcePool.java:40 stops being reachable from the network because
nothing structurally mutates it after boot.
BOTH LINES ARE REQUIRED AND THE .Size LINE IS THE LOAD-BEARING ONE.
ConnectionConfig.java:39 compiles (BufferPool\.\w+?\.)Size and iterates PROPERTY NAMES with
matcher.matches() at :87. `BufferPool.Huge.BufferSize` full-matches nothing (\w cannot span a
dot), so `.Size` is what DISCOVERS the pool; `.BufferSize` is only read at :92 from inside a
match, as group(1) + "BufferSize". A lone .BufferSize line registers NOTHING and this whole
mitigation silently does not exist. Gated by scripts/qa/public_host_checklist.py, which
demands the pair.
Why 65536: the largest dataSize the 2-byte header can express is 65535 - 2 = 65533, so 65536
is the smallest power of two that covers the entire representable range. Why 4: the residual
risk this leaves is TRANSIENT (one 64 KB in-flight buffer per hostile connection, released on
disconnect), which is a connection-count problem and belongs to SEC-2, not here.

THIS IS A SECURITY CONTROL, NOT A PERFORMANCE TIER. Do not delete it because it looks unused.
ReadHandler.handleHeader:92 reads the inbound packet length as
Short.toUnsignedInt(buffer.getShort()) - ConnectionConfig.HEADER_SIZE
and checks it only for > 0 at :93, so an attacker fully controls a dataSize in 1..65533 with
NO account, NO valid client, before decryption and before opcode dispatch, on BOTH the game
and login ports. That value reaches ResourcePool.determineBufferSize:153, and when
_bufferPools.ceilingEntry(size) returns null (:155) the engine MINTS A NEW PERMANENT POOL at
:168 which is never evicted. With the stock top tier at 32768, every size in 32769..65533 is
a distinct pool: 32,765 of them, each banking a direct buffer on disconnect
(Connection.close -> releaseReadingBuffer -> recycleBuffer -> BufferPool.recycle). Sum n for
n = 32769..65533 = 1,610,432,515 bytes = 1.50 GiB of off-heap memory, permanently, for about
65 KB of traffic: connect, send 2 bytes, hang up, repeat.
A pool whose BufferSize covers the WHOLE representable range means ceilingEntry never returns
null on the read path, so neither ResourcePool.determineBufferSize:168 nor
ResourcePool.getSizedBuffer:139 ever puts into the map from an inbound packet again. 32,765
permanent pools become one, ~1.5 GiB of permanent leak becomes 4 x 64 KB = 256 KB, and the
unsynchronised TreeMap at ResourcePool.java:40 stops being reachable from the network because
nothing structurally mutates it after boot.
BOTH LINES ARE REQUIRED AND THE .Size LINE IS THE LOAD-BEARING ONE.
ConnectionConfig.java:39 compiles (BufferPool\.\w+?\.)Size and iterates PROPERTY NAMES with
matcher.matches() at :87. `BufferPool.Huge.BufferSize` full-matches nothing (\w cannot span a
dot), so `.Size` is what DISCOVERS the pool; `.BufferSize` is only read at :92 from inside a
match, as group(1) + "BufferSize". A lone .BufferSize line registers NOTHING and this whole
mitigation silently does not exist. Gated by scripts/qa/public_host_checklist.py, which
demands the pair.
Why 65536: the largest dataSize the 2-byte header can express is 65535 - 2 = 65533, so 65536
is the smallest power of two that covers the entire representable range. Why 4: the residual
risk this leaves is TRANSIENT (one 64 KB in-flight buffer per hostile connection, released on
disconnect), which is a connection-count problem and belongs to SEC-2, not here.
